\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{خطيب} (khaṭīb)}{خطيب (khaṭīb)}]{\ar{خطيب} (khaṭīb) — a fiancé}

\label{lesson:AR-C528-khatib}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to go bankrupt, then the Arabic for to put aside.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{خطيب}}
\textbf{\ar{خطيب}} — \emph{khaṭīb} — \textquotedblleft{}a fiancé\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{زار} \ar{خطيب} \ar{أختي} \ar{بيتنا} \ar{أمس}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{zāra khaṭīb ukhtī baytanā ams.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My sister's fiancé visited our house yesterday.
\end{quote}

The same word also means a public speaker; \ar{خطيبة} is a fiancée.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{خطيب}} (\emph{khaṭīb}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{kh-ṭ-b}, \textquotedblleft{}to address; to ask in marriage\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives the root both senses: speaking to people and asking for a woman's hand.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{khaṭīb}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{khaṭīb}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{zāra khaṭīb ukhtī baytanā ams.} — My sister's fiancé visited our house yesterday.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to go bankrupt, then the Arabic for to put aside, then say \emph{khaṭīb} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{خطيب} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A fiancé\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{زواج} (zawāj)}{زواج (zawāj)}]{\ar{زواج} (zawāj) — marriage}

\label{lesson:AR-C528-zawaj}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for to put aside, then the Arabic for a fiancé.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{زواج}}
\textbf{\ar{زواج}} — \emph{zawāj} — \textquotedblleft{}marriage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{احتفل} \ar{جدي} \ar{وجدتي} \ar{بخمسين} \ar{سنة} \ar{من} \ar{الزواج}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{iḥtafala jaddī wa-jaddatī bi-khamsīna sana min az-zawāj.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My grandparents celebrated fifty years of marriage.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{زواج}} (\emph{zawāj}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{z-w-j}, \textquotedblleft{}a pair, one of a pair\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Zawj, a husband, and tazawwaja, to marry, which you know, are from the same root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{zawāj}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{zawāj}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{iḥtafala jaddī wa-jaddatī bi-khamsīna sana min az-zawāj.} — My grandparents celebrated fifty years of marriage.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for to put aside, then the Arabic for a fiancé, then say \emph{zawāj} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{زواج} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Marriage\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{حماة} (ḥamāh)}{حماة (ḥamāh)}]{\ar{حماة} (ḥamāh) — a mother-in-law}

\label{lesson:AR-C528-hamah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a fiancé, then the Arabic for marriage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{حماة}}
\textbf{\ar{حماة}} — \emph{ḥamāh} — \textquotedblleft{}a mother-in-law\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{تزور} \ar{حماتي} \ar{بيتنا} \ar{كل} \ar{جمعة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tazūru ḥamātī baytanā kull jumʿa.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My mother-in-law visits our house every Friday.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{حماة}} (\emph{ḥamāh}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ḥ-m-w}, \textquotedblleft{}a husband's or wife's kin\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives ḥam as the husband's father and ḥamāh as his mother.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ḥamāh}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tazūru ḥamātī baytanā kull jumʿa.} — My mother-in-law visits our house every Friday.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a fiancé, then the Arabic for marriage, then say \emph{ḥamāh} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{أعزب} (aʿzab)}{أعزب (aʿzab)}]{\ar{أعزب} (aʿzab) — single, unmarried}

\label{lesson:AR-C528-azab}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for marriage, then the Arabic for a mother-in-law.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{أعزب}}
\textbf{\ar{أعزب}} — \emph{aʿzab} — \textquotedblleft{}single, unmarried\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{أخي} \ar{الكبير} \ar{ما} \ar{زال} \ar{أعزب}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{akhī al-kabīr mā zāla aʿzab.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My older brother is still single.
\end{quote}

\ar{عزباء} is a single woman.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أعزب}} (\emph{aʿzab}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-z-b}, \textquotedblleft{}to be distant, remote\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives ʿazaba as to be far away: one far from marriage.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aʿzab}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aʿzab}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{akhī al-kabīr mā zāla aʿzab.} — My older brother is still single.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for marriage, then the Arabic for a mother-in-law, then say \emph{aʿzab} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{أعزب} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Single, unmarried\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{عشق} (ʿashiqa)}{عشق (ʿashiqa)}]{\ar{عشق} (ʿashiqa) — to love passionately}

\label{lesson:AR-C528-ashiqa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for a mother-in-law, then the Arabic for single.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{عشق}}
\textbf{\ar{عشق}} — \emph{ʿashiqa} — \textquotedblleft{}to love passionately\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{يعشق} \ar{جدي} \ar{الموسيقى} \ar{القديمة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{yaʿshaqu jaddī al-mūsīqā al-qadīma.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My grandfather adores old music.
\end{quote}

Present: \ar{يعشق}, \emph{yaʿshaq}.

The noun \ar{عشق} is passionate love.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عشق}} (\emph{ʿashiqa}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ʿ-sh-q}, \textquotedblleft{}to love passionately\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives yaʿshaqu as its present.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for a mother-in-law, then the Arabic for single, then say \emph{ʿashiqa} again
\end{itemize}
